terms.grammar: adverb: an old accusative of pars
evidence: Cic. Marc. 1: partim dolōre, partim verēcundiā (Lewis & Short)
Cic. Q. fr. 1.3.5: amīcī partim dēseruerint mē, partim etiam prōdiderint (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Most often doubled, partim … partim, “partly … partly”, and with persons “some … others” (amīcī partim … partim, some of my friends … others). In Plautus and Cato it can mean “for the most part” (Lewis & Short).

evidence: Cic. Q. fr. 3.1.9: ex parte gaudeō (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: With an adjective it gives the degree: aliquā ex parte, to some extent; magnā ex parte, largely (see largely); nē minimā quidem ex parte, not in the least (Cic. Off. 1.76, Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: diūturnī silentiī … nōn timōre aliquō, sed partim dolōre, partim verēcundiā, fīnem hodiernus diēs attulit
phrases.english: today has brought an end to a long silence, kept not from any fear but partly from grief, partly from diffidence

phrases.latin: multa ab animālium vōcibus trālāta in hominēs, partim quae sunt aperta, partim obscūra
phrases.english: many words have been carried over from the cries of animals to people, some of them plain, some obscure

phrases.latin: dīcere etiam solēbat nūllum esse librum tam malum ut nōn aliquā parte prōdesset
phrases.english: he used to say, too, that no book was so bad that it was not useful in some part
